title: The passive in depth
goal: Read and use the passive the way Indonesians really do: di- with its -kan and -i endings, the "type 2" passive with a pronoun (sudah saya baca), and ter- for what happens by accident, what can be done, and what simply is.
bekal: understand official passives like *dikenakan biaya, dikelola oleh, dilarang*
answer naturally with the pronoun passive: *Sudah saya baca. Akan kami ajukan.*
tell apart the three jobs of ter-: *terbawa arus, terjangkau, tertulis*

notes: **Rancangan peraturan desa.** A *rancangan* is a draft (from *rancang*, to design), and a *peraturan desa*, usually shortened to *Perdes*, is a village regulation with legal force. It is divided into *pasal* (articles) and *ayat* (clauses). You will meet the same words in national law in B2.

**Sudah saya baca.** Asked "has it been read?", Sarah answers with the pronoun passive: "already by-me read". This is how Indonesians naturally report what they have done to something already under discussion. *Saya sudah membacanya* is correct but sounds slightly stiff here.

**Dikenakan biaya sebesar...** — "is charged a fee of". *Mengenakan* means "to impose" (and also "to wear"), so *dikenakan biaya* is the formula on every official tariff. *Sebesar* ("to the size of") introduces an amount of money: *denda sebesar Rp500.000* (a fine of 500,000 rupiah).

**Tanpa didampingi pemandu** — "without being accompanied by a guide". After *tanpa* (without), Indonesian happily uses a passive verb where English needs "being": *tanpa diundang* (uninvited), *tanpa dibayar* (unpaid). Note the agent follows directly, with no *oleh*.

**Dikeramatkan, Mbah.** *Keramat* means sacred, spiritually powerful; *dikeramatkan* is "regarded as sacred". Many Javanese villages have the grave of a founding figure, often called *Mbah* (grandparent, elder), where people pray and leave flowers. Visitors are welcome, but only with respect and a local guide.

**Waduh, maklum.** *Waduh* is "oh dear, oh no", mild and a little comic. *Maklum* means "understandable, you know how it is", used to excuse something small: *Maklum, desa* (well, it's a village). It asks the listener to be forgiving, and they usually are.

grammars.title: di-, di-…-kan, di-…-i: the ending comes along
body: The passive keeps whatever ending the active verb had. If the active is *menjelaskan*, the passive is *dijelaskan*; if it is *mengawasi*, the passive is *diawasi*. Nothing new to learn, only to carry across.
after: *Oleh* (by) is optional, and after a di- verb the agent can simply follow: *disepakati warga* (agreed by the residents). Formal documents tend to keep *oleh*; speech drops it or uses *sama*.

⚠️ Some pairs differ only in the ending: *dikenakan biaya* (a fee is imposed) but *dikenai biaya* (someone is charged a fee). Both appear in real regulations, and both are correct; the *-i* form puts the person in subject position.

grammars.title: The pronoun passive ("type 2")
body: When the doer is *saya, kami, kita, Anda* or a title used as "you", Indonesian prefers to put the pronoun straight before the bare root, with no prefix: object + (marker) + pronoun + root.

head: Indonesian
Word for word
English
rows: We'll submit it to the council.
There's something we need to discuss.
You must fill in this form.

after: The order is fixed: the markers *sudah, akan, harus, bisa, belum, tidak* come **before** the pronoun. ✗ *Saya sudah baca* is active, not this pattern; ✗ *Saya baca sudah* is wrong.
For *dia* and *mereka* formal writing uses *di-* instead: *Surat itu ditulisnya sendiri*, *dibaca oleh mereka*. In speech, *dia tulis* and *mereka baca* are common and accepted.

notes: **Terbawa arus** — "carried off by the current". This is the accidental *ter-*: nobody intended it and there is no agent. Compare *dibawa* (carried, by someone, on purpose). You met this *ter-* in A2 with *tertinggal* and *terjatuh*; here it meets a flood.

**Ada yang terluka?** — "is anyone hurt?", literally "is there one who is injured?". *Ada yang* + verb is the everyday way to say "anyone, someone": *Ada yang mau kopi?* (anyone for coffee?). *Astaga* is "good heavens", surprise or alarm, polite enough for anyone.

**Ditutup sama warga.** In speech *sama* replaces *oleh* for the agent of a passive: *dimarahin sama ibu* (told off by Mum). It also means "with" and "same", so context does the work. In writing, always *oleh*.

**Udah aku telepon.** The pronoun passive in its spoken form, with *aku* and *udah*. Yoga's sentence is exactly the pattern Sarah used with Pak Harun, *Sudah saya baca*, just turned down to casual volume.

**Kelihatan, and aja nggak.** *Kelihatan* is the everyday word for *terlihat* (visible, can be seen). *X aja nggak* means "not even X": *Ujungnya aja nggak kelihatan* (you can't even see the end). The formal version is *X saja tidak* or *bahkan X pun tidak*.

**Dilewati, biar.** *Melewati* is "to pass through, go along", so *jalan yang bisa dilewati* is "a road that can be passed along". *Biar* is spoken *supaya* or *agar* (so that). A2 Unit 12 had *supaya*; you will hear *biar* ten times as often.

grammars.title: Three jobs of ter-
body: *Ter-* never has a doer in sight. Within that, it does three different jobs, and the context nearly always tells you which.
after: The ability meaning is the one learners miss. *Harganya terjangkau* is not "the price has been reached" but "the price can be reached", in other words affordable. Advertisements love it: *harga terjangkau, lokasi strategis*.
💬 In speech, ability *ter-* often becomes *ke-…-an*: *terlihat* becomes *kelihatan*, *terdengar* becomes *kedengaran*, *terbaca* becomes *kebaca*.

blocks.text: Regulations, notices and contracts are written almost entirely in the passive, because the institution speaks and nobody in particular acts. These fixed lines turn up in any Indonesian document.

*Barang yang sudah dibeli tidak dapat dikembalikan.*

blocks.text: You do not need to write like this yet, but reading it is a B1 skill. Find the di- verb first; it almost always carries the meaning of the whole sentence.
Indonesian has several ways to say that something was done. Choosing is simpler than it looks: ask who the doer is, and whether anyone meant to do it.

blocks.title: Why Indonesians love the passive
items: It keeps the topic first: the bridge, the letter, the regulation. English likes to start with the person; Indonesian likes to start with the thing being talked about.
It is polite: *Sudah dibayar?* (has it been paid?) asks without pointing a finger at anyone.
A good habit for you: when your English sentence starts "I have ..." about a thing already mentioned, try *Sudah saya ...* instead.
